packs.title: Forest, Makers & Monuments
packs.promise: Meet Mexico City through Chapultepec, Coyoacán and the silhouettes of Reforma.

q.s: Collect three plant shapes without picking a thing.
st: Enter the botanical garden Tuesday–Sunday during its confirmed daytime opening, aiming to finish before 16:00. In an open collection area, find three visibly different plant shapes, such as a thick leaf, a narrow leaf and a branching form.
Read one available label and record the name exactly, or describe its location and shape if the label is missing.
Beside each shape, note how it catches light or holds shadow. Do not infer a medicinal use or water need from appearance.
Choose the shape you could recognize again and describe its outline in one line.

q.s: Make a small record that separates seeing from knowing.
st: Enter Tuesday–Sunday around noon with valid admission: MXN 210 general, or the applicable reduced/free entry. Sunday free entry applies to Mexican nationals and foreign residents with the required identification; other documented eligible free visits count too. Use the museum map to choose one open archaeology gallery and one open ethnography gallery. Allow 100 minutes plus queues before 18:00 closing.
In each, select an object with a readable label. Record its name and the community, place or period the label gives; leave missing information unknown.
Make a field card with two boxes for each object: “Visible details” for an outline or three observed features, and “Label evidence” for one sourced fact.
Add a question the display leaves you with. Compare how much your outline could explain without the label.

q.s: Turn a material observation into your own small design.
st: For the combined outing, enter Tuesday–Friday around 13:00 with valid admission: MXN 22 general, or free entry for under-12s or holders of student, teacher or INAPAM credentials. Choose an open exhibition’s labelled work identifying its maker or community and material. Finish before 18:00; exhibitions change rather than forming a guaranteed permanent display.
Look for one visible choice about joining, shaping or arranging the material. Compare your observation with any process information the display provides.
Design a small container for an everyday item you carry. Use a quick sketch or three sentences to explain its shape, material and opening.
Name the exhibited work that prompted you, then label your design as your own. Borrow a practical question, not a sacred form or a maker’s distinctive motif.

packs.title: Centro in Detail
packs.promise: Explore Centro Histórico through a mural, tiled walls, civic facades and archaeological evidence.

q.s: Use Rivera’s arrangement to plan a scene of your own.
st: Begin around noon Tuesday–Sunday with valid museum admission: pay the applicable fee (MXN 45 general) or use documented free entry, including free admission for everyone on Sunday. Read Rivera’s mural title and artist, then look across its left, centre and right sections from an open visitor position. Allow the hour-long activity plus queues; the museum closes at 18:00.
Choose one visible way Rivera gathers figures or separates a group. Describe the arrangement without inventing identities for the people shown.
Make your own three-panel scene of an imagined afternoon in a public square. Use a sketch if permitted, or one sentence for each panel.
Give your scene a title and name Rivera’s mural as the prompt. Keep your invented scene separate from the mural’s historical interpretation.

q.s: Read a working post office from the street.
st: Find an open pavement position facing the Postal Palace without blocking its doors.
Collect three different exterior details: a clock or other time clue, an elaborate opening or arch, and a small repeated ornament. Describe what is visible if a sign or clock is obscured.
Choose a detail that seems practical and one that seems decorative. Explain your choices as observations, not statements about the architect’s intention.
Write one line that pairs the building’s continuing postal job with what you noticed on its facade.

q.s: Make a tiny plan of the Zócalo from its open edge.
st: Choose an open perimeter viewpoint where you can see at least two sides of the square without blocking movement.
Draw a simple rectangle or describe four edges in words. Place the Cathedral to the north and National Palace to the east using the view and a map if needed; mark unseen edges as unseen.
Add one feature you actually notice at two different heights, such as an opening near the pavement and a roofline above.
Write a caption for your own plan about how large the square feels from this edge. Your caption describes this visit, not a fixed fact about the square.
